this stage with the expectation that the State Government shall
formulate a separate Memorandum of Settlement for the claim of
respondent No.5 for which the Member Secretary of the Tamil Nadu
State Legal Services Authority shall prepare a draft module in
consultation with the State Government which may be acceptable to
respondent No.5 also.  We hope and trust that the claim of the said
respondent shall also be settled within three months.

O R D E R
This is a petition filed under Section 25 of the Code of
Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short “CPC”) by the petitioner, who
is the wife of the respondent.
2. The petitioner has filed this transfer petition seeking
the following reliefs:
“a) Transfer the Matrimonial Case No.2939 of 2024
filed under Section 10 of the Hindu Marriage Act,
1955  preferred  by  the  respondent  -  Sahil
Chhibbar, pending before the Court of Principal
Judge, Family Court, Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh to
the Family Court, 6 th Floor, City Civil Court
Building, Bhadra, Ahmedabad District, Gujarat, in
the interest of justice, or 
b) pass such other further order(s) as this
Hon’ble Court may deem fit and proper in the
facts and circumstances  of the  present case
and in the interest of justice.”
1

## Page 256

3. During the pendency of this petition, the parties were
referred to the Supreme Court Mediation Centre in order to
explore the possibility of a settlement between them.  
4. Learned counsel for the respective parties, who were
appearing through Video Conferencing facility submitted
that parties have arrived at a settlement. The Settlement
Agreement has been drawn up on 29.06.2026, a copy of which
is placed on record. The parties have decided to part ways
and seek  dissolution of their marriage by a decree of
divorce by mutual consent. Hence, an application  under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India has been filed.  
5. Learned counsel for the respective parties submitted
that the settlement agreement as well as the application
filed jointly  under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India by the parties may be taken on record and orders may
be made with regard to dissolution of the marriage between
the parties by a decree of divorce by mutual consent as per
the terms of the settlement.
6. The parties have appeared before this Court through
the Video Conferencing facility.  They have been identified
by their respective counsel.  We have also interacted with
the parties. When we queried as to whether they intended to
2

## Page 257

part ways, the parties stated that they have indeed agreed
to seek  dissolution of their marriage by a decree of
divorce by mutual consent  and hence have filed a joint
application  under Article 142 of the Constitution of
India.  They further stated that they have arrived at the
settlement before the Supreme Court Mediation Centre  on
their own free volition,  without there  being  any
coercion  or undue influence from any side. They also
stated that they have already complied with the terms of
the  settlement  and  they  would  also  comply  with  the
settlement agreement in future. 
7. In  the  above  backdrop,  the  Settlement  Agreement
dated 29.06.2026  and the joint application filed by the
parties  under Article 142 of the Constitution of India are
taken on record.
8. Learned counsel for the parties submitted that the
cases earlier filed by the parties have been withdrawn and
Matrimonial Case No.2939 of 2024 filed by the respondent
before  the  Court  of  Principal  Judge,  Family  Court,
Ghaziabad, Uttar Pradesh has to be disposed of.
9. Further, we note that a sum of Rs.30,00,000/- (Rupees
Thirty lakhs) has been paid by the respondent to the
petitioner for the educational and living expenses of their
3

## Page 258

minor son Master Haneesh who is presently five years of
age.  The custody of minor son shall remain with the
petitioner/mother subject to the visitation rights of the
respondent.  There are other terms and conditions which
have  been  stated  in  the  Settlement  Agreement  dated
29.06.2026.  
10. The parties have stated that they would abide by the
said terms and conditions. 
11. We have perused the terms of the Settlement Agreement
dated 29.06.2026 and we find that the same are lawful and
there is no legal impediment in accepting the same.  We
have also perused the joint application filed by the
parties under Article 142. We also note that the parties
seek dissolution of their marriage a decree of divorce by
mutual consent.
12. In the circumstances, the  joint application filed
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India is allowed.
The marriage between the petitioner and the respondent
solemnised on 31.01.2020 at Noida, Uttar Pradesh stands
dissolved by a decree of divorce by mutual consent.
13. In view of the aforesaid order, Matrimonial Case No.2939
of 2024 shall stand disposed of. 
4

## Page 259

14. The Settlement Agreement dated 29.06.2026 shall be
read as a part and parcel of this order.
15. The Transfer Petition stands disposed of accordingly.

O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the
parties.
3. This  appeal  arises  from  an  order
dated 25.02.2026 passed by the High Court of
Punjab and Haryana at Chandigarh rejecting
the regular bail prayer of the appellant in
connection with FIR No. 21/2020, registered
at P.S. Kotbhai, District Sri Muktsar Sahib.
4. At  the  outset,  the  submission  on
behalf of the appellant is that he has
suffered pending trial incarceration since
04.02.2020. Two additional accused have been
added under Section 319 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973 which has resulted
1

## Page 288

in delay of the trial. Besides, one revolver
is said to have been used by as many as four
accused. The said revolver is licenced to
appellant’s father Rajveer Singh, who is
also an accused. In such circumstances, it
has been submitted that the appellant, who
has no previous criminal antecedents, is
entitled to be released on bail.  
5. The learned Counsel for the State-
respondent has opposed the prayer for bail
but could not point out anything material to
the contrary. 
6. In such circumstances, having regard
to  the  period  of  incarceration  pending
trial, we are of the view that the appellant
is entitled to be released on bail pending
trial. 
7. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
The order passed by the High Court rejecting
the regular bail prayer of the appellant is
set aside.
8. The appellant shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as the
2

## Page 289

trial court may deem fit to impose in the
facts and circumstances of the case.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

IRFAAN @ MUNNA @ KABUTAR           APPELLANT
                        VERSUS
STATE OF RAJASTHAN                      RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The jurisdictional police intercepted an Alto Car on
29.12.2025 on a check post of Delhi by-pass road, Jaipur on a tip-
off and found Mr. Arjun Lal Gurjar was in conscious possession of
13.33 grams (net weight) of smack in his shirt pocket and it was
seized at the spot. It is the case of the prosecution that  said
accused – Mr. Arjun Lal Gurjar had confessed to the Police that
contraband had been sold by the appellant herein for Rs.30,000/-
(Rupees Thirty Thousand only) and based on the said co-accused
1

## Page 293

statement appellant had been roped in which was supported by
call data records, namely, a conversation which had occurred just
prior to the seizure.
4. One intriguing factor which can be noticed in the instant
case is immediately after seizure memo being drawn, the co-
accused, Mr. Arjun Lal Gurjar when questioned about source of
the contraband at the time of his arrest, has stated that it was
procured from one ‘Hakhla’ of Nai ki Thadi. Hence, it is for the
prosecution to establish as to the role of the appellant which can
be connected to the contraband that was seized from the co-
accused – Arjun Lal Gurjar. It is no doubt true that learned
counsel for the respondent – State submitted that the appellant
is also having antecedents of similar nature. However, it is for the
prosecution to prove the complexity of the appellant in the
instant case. Charge sheet having been filed, we are of the
considered view that the continued incarceration of the appellant
would not be warranted. Hence, the appeal is allowed and
appellant is ordered to be released on regular bail on such terms
and conditions as the jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose
2

## Page 294

including the condition of directing him to appear before the trial
court on all dates of hearing except when exempted. 
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION (C) NO. 3437 OF 2025
MOHINI SHAW                                        PETITIONER
                                VERSUS
ANIL KUMAR                                          RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. In course of hearing of this transfer petition, the petitioner-wife (Ms.
Mohini Shaw) and the respondent-husband (Anil Kumar) were referred to the
Supreme Court Mediation Centre.
2. The process of mediation has produced positive results. The Mediator
has sent a report that the parties have agreed to resolve their inter  se
disputes and differences amicably. It has also been decided by them to apply
before this Court seeking dissolution of their marriage by mutual consent
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India.
3. The parties have jointly filed an application (IA No. 258669 of 2026)
under Article 142 of the Constitution of India, in view of such settlement. The
prayers in the application under Article 142 read as follows:
“A) Pass an order granting divorce to both the parties by exercising the
powers granted by Article 142 of the Constitution of India to this Hon’ble
Court to achieve ‘complete justice’;
B) pass any other order(s)/directions, which this Hon’ble Court may deem fit
and proper in the facts and circumstances of the case.”
 

## Page 308

2
4. Summary of the terms of settlement found in paragraph 5 of the
application reads as follows:
“A. That the parties have agreed that the Respondent-husband will pay
to the Petitioner-wife a total sum of Rs. 21,00,000/- (Rupees
Twenty One Laklıs Only) towards full and final settlement of all
her  claims  towards  her  permanent  alimony,  Stridhan,
maintenance  (past,  present,  future)  and  any  other  claim
whatsoever. 
B. It is agreed between the parties that they will move an application
jointly before the Hon'ble Supreme Court under Article 142 of
Constitution of India for invoking inherent powers of the Hon'ble
Supreme Court praying for divorce by mutual consent as parties
are staying separately since 09.09.2021 i.e. for the last more than
five years and there is irretrievable break down of the marriage. 
C.  It is further agreed between the parties that if Hon'ble Supreme
Court is pleased to allow application filed by both the parties
under Article 142 of Constitution of India then both the parties
shall withdraw the all the cases filed by them against each other.
The Respondent-husband will pay to the Petitioner/ Wife a total
sum of Rs. 21,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty One Lakhs Only) via
Demand Draft in the name of Petitioner/wife.
D.   The Respondent-husband will pay an amount of Rs. 21,00,000/-
(Rupees Twenty One Lakhs Only) in 2 installments is as under:-
I. The Respondent -husband has paid first installment an amount
of Rs. 2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakhs only) in favour of the
Petitioner/ wife by way of demand draft bearing No. 069031
dated 30.07.2026, State Bank of India, at the time of signing of
the present Settlement Agreement i.e. 10.08.2026.
II.  The Respondent-husband shall pay Second installment an
amount of Rs. 19,00,000/- (Rupees Nineteen Lakhs only) in
favour of the Petitioner/wife by way of demand draft before the
Court at the time of final hearing of Joint Application Under
Article 142 Constitution of India.”
5. The petitioner-wife has joined the proceedings virtually from Kolkata.
The respondent-husband is present in Court. Responding to our query, they
have separately submitted that the settlement has been arrived at by them
voluntarily and there has been no undue influence or pressure from any side.
6. The parties having amicably resolved the  inter  se  disputes and
differences, the terms of settlement which are contained in the joint

## Page 309

3
application shall form part of this order.
7. Accordingly, in exercise of power conferred on us by Article 142 of the
Constitution  of India , we dissolve the marriage between the parties by
mutual consent by granting an order in terms of prayer (A) of the joint
application under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. Decree be
drawn up, accordingly.
8. We record that Demand Draft No. 069043 dated 11 th August, 2026 for
Rs.19,00,000/- [Rupees nineteen lakh only] has been handed over to learned
counsel appearing for the petitioner-wife towards full and final settlement of
her dues. Photocopy of such demand draft shall be retained with the records.
9. Now that payment in terms of the settlement has been made and
accepted, we record that the parties have no subsisting claim against each
other.
10. As a result of this order, nothing survives for decision on the transfer
petition. The transfer petition stands disposed of together with IA No. 258669
of 2026.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
12. The proceedings from which this transfer petition arose shall stand
closed.

with two minor daughters aged 12 years and 6 years respectively,
who are currently residing with the petitioner-wife. While the

being so, it will be more convenient for the parties if the pending

O R D E R
1. The  instant  petition  under  Section  11(6)  of  the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (1996 Act), seeks the
appointment of a Sole Arbitrator to adjudicate disputes
arising  from  the  Amended  Employment  Contract  dated
16.04.2013  (Employment  Agreement)  executed  between  the
Petitioner and Aptar Pharma India Private Limited (Aptar
India/Respondent  No.  1),  to  which  AptarGroup,  Inc.
(Respondent No. 2) is also claimed to be a signatory and a
veritable party.
2. Briefly observed, the Petitioner is an Indian citizen,
who was appointed as a Director of Respondent No. 1 on
22.02.2008,  and  was  subsequently  appointed  as  General
1

## Page 318

Manager  and  Vice  President  of  Aptar  Pharma,  India  and
Southeast Asia, vide the Amended Employment Contract dated
16.04.2013. Respondent No. 1 is a private limited company
incorporated  under  the  Companies  Act,  1956  having  its
registered office at Navi Mumbai, Maharashtra. Respondent
No. 2 is a company incorporated in Delaware, USA, and is the
parent company of Respondent No. 1, which is its wholly
owned subsidiary.
3. During the subsistence of his employment with Respondent
No. 1, the Petitioner was granted stock options in the form
of Restricted Stock Units (RSUs) and Performance Stock Units
(PSUs) by Respondent No. 2 under Stock Option Agreements
dated 20.01.2010, 11.01.2012 and 10.02.2017. These stock
options were granted under the Stock Awards Plan and Equity
Incentive  Plan  in  connection  with  his  employment  with
Respondent No. 1. However, the Petitioner’s employment with
Respondent No. 1 ceased with effect from 30.06.2022.
4. The  disputes  between  the  parties  arose  shortly
thereafter. The Petitioner’s case is that, upon cessation of
employment, the Respondents illegally forfeited the above-
stated stock options that had vested in his favour on the
ground that he had subsequently secured employment with
another  entity,  which  the  Respondents  treated  as  a
“Competing  Entity.”  It  is  further  alleged  that  the
Respondents failed to pay the non-compete compensation due
to the Petitioner under Sub-clause 11.4 of the Employment
2

## Page 319

Agreement.
5. The Petitioner, thus, issued a Notice of Arbitration
dated 26.03.2025 to the Respondents under Clause 15.5 of the
Employment Agreement, proposing the name of Justice Akil
Kureshi, Former Chief Justice of Rajasthan High Court as the
Sole  Arbitrator.  The  Respondents,  by  their  reply  dated
25.04.2025, rejected the invocation of arbitration, and the
Respondent No.2 specifically contested that it is not bound
by the arbitration clause, as it was not a signatory to the
Employment  Agreement.  The  said  response  prompted  the
Petitioner to file the instant Arbitration Petition.
6. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and
perused the material placed on record.
7. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances recorded
above and the relevant provision(s) under the Employment
Agreement, we deem it just and proper to allow the instant
Arbitration  Petition  and  appoint  Mr.  Nitin  G.  Thakker
(Senior Advocate and President, Bombay Bar Association) as
the Sole Arbitrator to adjudicate the disputes between the
parties. The seat and venue of arbitration, in accordance
with the arbitration agreement, shall be Mumbai, India.
Ordered accordingly.
8. We make it clear that the parties will be at liberty to
raise all available contentions before the learned Sole
Arbitrator.
3

## Page 320

9. The learned Sole Arbitrator shall have the liberty to
fix his own remuneration/fees. 
10. Pending interlocutory applications, if any, also stand
disposed of.

1. These special leave petitions are directed against the order
dated 02.05.2024 passed by the Learned Special Judge, (PC Act)
(CBI), Coal Block Cases-02, Rouse Avenue District Courts, New
2

## Page 329

Delhi. Vide the said order, the learned Special Judge has charged
some  of  the  accused,  whereas  some  other  accused  have  been
discharged. The Enforcement Directorate, being aggrieved against
complete discharge of some of the accused persons, approached this
Court  in  SLP(Crl.)  No.14346/2026,  which  was  disposed  of  on
29.07.2026, relegating the Enforcement Directorate to approach the
High Court of Delhi.
2. The instant special leave petitions, arising out of the same
order, are at the instance of those accused who have been charged
by the Special Court. Since a part of the subject impugned order is
already under challenge before the Delhi High Court, albeit at the
instance of the Enforcement Directorate, we are of the opinion that
possibility of conflicting orders ought to be avoided.
3. In this view of the matter, the petitioners can also be
relegated to the High Court of Delhi by transferring these special
leave petitions to be treated as Criminal Revision Petitions by the
High Court. 
4. At this stage, it is pointed out by the learned Special Public
Prosecutor, appearing for the Enforcement Directorate, that in view
of the judgment of this Court in Girish  Kumar  Suneja v. Central
Bureau of Investigation reported in (2017) 14 SCC 809, reiterating
the first order in Manohar Lal Sharma  v. The Principal Secretary &
Ors. reported in (2015) 13 SCC 35, any application seeking stay of
the trial proceedings would be maintainable only before this Court
and not before the High Court.
5. Following the said dictum, we direct that no interim stay on
the pending trial shall be granted by the High Court. However,
3

## Page 330

keeping in view the fact that conclusion of trial can prejudice the
petitioners, we request the High Court to decide the transferred
cases expeditiously and preferably within four months. 
6. It is clarified that we have not expressed any opinion on
merits of these petitions.
7. The Special Leave Petitions are, accordingly, disposed of.
8. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.4131/2026
(@Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (Crl.)  No.13162/2026)
VIJAY KUMAR                                        Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH                          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal arises out of the impugned final judgment
and order dated 03.12.2025 passed by the High Court of Himachal
Pradesh, Shimla, in Cr.MP (M) No. 2264 of 2025, whereby the regular
bail application preferred by the appellant in connection with FIR
No.  120/2023  dated  24.09.2023,  registered  at  Police  Station
Palampur,  District  Kangra,  Himachal  Pradesh,  for  offences
punishable under Sections 420 and 120-B of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 (IPC), Section 5 of the Himachal Pradesh Protection of
Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1999, and
Sections 21 and 23 of the Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes
Act, 2019, was rejected.
3. The learned Senior Counsel for the appellant submits that the
appellant was neither named in the original FIR dated 24.09.2023
nor alleged by any investor/depositor to have induced investments
or operated the fraudulent cryptocurrency platform/scheme. The

## Page 338

2
primary allegation against the appellant stems from transactions in
immovable  properties  and  commercial  dealings  with  the  main
co-accused,  Subhash  Sharma.  The  appellant  surrendered  on
07.03.2025, was remanded to police custody, and has remained in
judicial custody since 17.03.2025. The Supplementary Charge-sheet
under Section 173 Cr.P.C./ Section 193 BNSS has already been filed
on  08.05.2025,  and  the  investigation  qua  the  appellant  is
substantially complete and largely based on documentary evidence.
4. Per contra, the learned counsel for the State has opposed the
grant of bail, contending that the case involves an economic
offence of huge magnitude involving public funds collected under
the guise of cryptocurrency multi-level marketing schemes. The main
mastermind, Subhash Sharma, has absconded and is suspected to have
fled abroad.
5. Having considered the rival submissions, the period of custody
undergone by the appellant (in detention since March 2025), the
completion  of  investigation  followed  by  the  filing  of  the
supplementary  charge-sheet,  and  the  fact  that  the  primary
allegations regarding direct inducement of investors pertain to
other named accused, we are of the view that continued pre-trial
detention of the appellant is not warranted, subject to stringent
conditions to secure his presence during trial. Accordingly, the
impugned Order dated 03.12.2025 passed by the High Court of
Himachal Pradesh is set aside. The appellant, Vijay Kumar, is
ordered to be released on regular bail in connection with FIR
No.120/2023 registered at Police Station Palampur, District Kangra,
Himachal Pradesh, subject to terms and conditions that the trial

## Page 339

3
court may deem fit and proper to impose. The trial court shall
ensure that the passport of the appellant is surrendered, if not
already surrendered, and make it incumbent on the appellant to take
permission of that Court to travel out of the State of Punjab. The
appellant shall also appear before the I.O. every Monday for 6
months and then as required by the trial court.
6. It is brought to our notice that the main co-accused, Subhash
Sharma,  who  is  key  to  the  operation  of  the  multi-level
cryptocurrency scheme and diversion of funds, has absconded and is
reported to be residing outside India (alleged to be in Dubai/UAE).
7. The Respondent-State of Himachal Pradesh and the Special
Investigation  Team  (SIT),  through  the  Central  Bureau  of
Investigation (CBI - National Central Bureau, New Delhi) and the
Ministry of Home Affairs/Ministry of External Affairs, Government
of India, are directed to forthwith initiate all necessary steps
for the issuance and execution of appropriate notices against
co-accused Subhash Sharma to facilitate his arrest and extradition
to India to face trial.
8. Attachment  of  Assets:  The  Competent  Authority  under  the
Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019 (BUDS Act) and the
HP Protection of Interest of Depositors Act, 1999, along with the
SIT, shall take immediate steps for provisional attachment and
final confirmation of attachment of all movable and immovable
properties, bank accounts, and commercial holdings held in the name
of  co-accused  Subhash  Sharma,  his  family  members,  or  benami
entities, wherever situated, in accordance with law and that of the
appellant herein where it is suspected of having been purchased out

## Page 340

4
of the proceeds of this crime.
9. We also request the Chief Justice of the High Court to
constitute a Special Court to exclusively deal with the captioned
crime, since it involves 80,000 investors who together have lost
around Rs.20,000 Crores, as and when requested by the Investigating
Officer.
10. With the aforesaid, the appeal is disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.

FACTS
We  have  heard  learned  counsel  for  the
appellant and learned Additional Advocate General
for the respondent-State. We have also perused the
material on record.
Learned counsel for the appellant submitted
that for the purpose of seeking modification in the
sentence imposed on the appellant herein, so as to
convert the same into one of fine both under
Section 304-A of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and
Section 187 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the
appellant has deposited an amount of Rs.3,00,000/-
before the Trial court (Court of Senior Civil Judge
and  Judicial  Magistrate  First  Class  at
1

## Page 343

Thirthahalli) in Criminal Case No.328 of 2016. In
the circumstances, the punishment of imprisonment
may be set aside and converted to one of payment of
fine to only both the aforesaid provisions and
consequently, the said amount of Rs.3,00,000/- may
be paid to the claimants being the dependants of
the deceased.
Learned  AAG  appearing  for  the  State  of
Karnataka submitted that appropriate orders may be
made in the case having regard to the fact that the
appellant has deposited a sum of Rs.3,00,000/-
before the Trial Court. 
Consequently,  we  find  that  the  ends  of
justice would be met in this case if the order of
punishment with regard to the Simple imprisonment
for a period of six months and for one month under
the aforesaid two provisions i.e.., Section 304-A
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and Section 187 of
the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, is modified and
instead, the punishment one of fine only is imposed
and the fine shall be Rs.3,00,000/- under both the
aforesaid provisions.
Since  the  said  amount  has  already  been

deposited by the appellant before the Trial Court,
we direct the Trial Court to issue notice to the

occurred  on  15.04.2014  when  the  appellant  was
riding the lorry which caused the accident.

rejected.
5.  Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submitted  that  the
appellant is the complainant in the original case, in which

## Page 356

2
respondent No.2 was granted bail. Subsequent thereto, respondent
No.2 threatened the witnesses, for which another substantive FIR
was lodged while he was in jail in which he was granted bail by the
High Court vide order dated 04.08.2025. The appellant thus moved
the High Court for cancellation of the bail granted to respondent
No.2 in the second case on the ground of threats issued by him to
the petitioner after being released on bail in the original case
filed by the appellant.
6. It was submitted that though the Court has accepted that there
has been a violation of the terms of the bail granted, it has, in
the same breath, also been held that this would not be a sufficient
ground for cancellation of bail. It was further contended that even
otherwise, the bail granted was misplaced and erroneous, for the
reason that respondent No.2 has 19 other criminal antecedents.
7. Learned counsel for the respondent No.1-State of Rajasthan
submitted that they have been regularly taking action against the
respondent No.2 but he is a habitual offender and thus the learned
counsel submitted that the State was also fully supporting the
contentions of the learned counsel for the appellant and would pray
that bail be cancelled.
8. As there is no representation on behalf of respondent No.2 and
no counter affidavit has been filed, the Court finds that the
allegations made by the appellant, for which there is factual basis
and which are supported by the State, there is no reason to
disbelieve the allegations regarding the conduct of respondent No.2

## Page 357

3
post grant of bail in the first substantive FIR.
9. We note here with some discomfort that the reasoning given by
the High Court in the impugned order, especially at paragraph No.
10, where despite the Court accepting the violation of the terms
and conditions of the bail, it has still held that it would not be
sufficient for cancellation of bail. We find the same to be not
only misplaced, but also unfounded and unsustainable.
10. Accordingly, on the short point that the reasoning given for
non-interference, as also on merits, is not sustainable, the appeal
is allowed. The bail granted to respondent No.2 vide High Court’s
order dated 04.08.2025 is cancelled. Respondent No.2 is directed to
surrender latest within two weeks from today, failing which the
State shall ensure that he is arrested and produced before the
Court for being taken into judicial custody.
11. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.
......................J.
(AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH)
......................J.
(MANMOHAN)

2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal is preferred against the order order dated
17.02.2026 in BA No. 2450/2025 passed by the High Court of
Judicature at Bombay at Aurangabad, by which the prayer for bail of
the appellant had been rejected.
4. The appellant is accused in connection with FIR No. 97/2022
dated 20.03.2022 registered with Chakur P.S., District Latur,
Maharashtra for the offences punishable under Sections 302 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short “IPC”) and after filing of
charge-sheet on September 2022, Sections 201, 120-B, 212, 216 read
with Section 34 of the IPC and Sections 3(1)(i), 3(2), 3(3), 3(4)
of the Maharashtra Control of Organised Crimes Act were added.
5. The basic allegation against the appellant is of murder of an

## Page 360

2
unidentified person, whose body was found, with injuries caused by
a sharp edged weapon . Learned counsel for the appellant submitted
that the appellant is in custody for almost 4½ years and has no
criminal antecedent except relating to the same crime and the trial
has not yet started, as the charges have not been framed.
6. Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Maharashtra
submitted that the daily roznama discloses that the delay is due to
the other accused, who are on some pretext or the other, delaying
the framing of charge and thus, the prosecution is not to blame for
the same. However, he fairly submitted that such delay could not be
attributed to the appellant, as he is behind the bars.
7. Taking into account the circumstances of the case, the period
of custody undergone by the appellant and the fact that the trial
has not yet commenced,  and an overall view of the matter, we are
inclined to  allow the prayer for bail . Accordingly, the appeal
stands allowed and the appellant is granted bail on the conditions
as imposed by the Trial Court, with an additional condition that
the appellant shall cooperate with the investigation/trial.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.             OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (C) NO. 18468 OF 2026)
STATE OF TAMIL NADU & ORS. ...Appellants
                                VERSUS
D. PAULRAJ & ANR.         ...Respondents
O R D E R
1) Leave granted.
2) We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties.
3) We are dealing with a case involving the appointment
of  an  unsubsidised  vocational  Instructor  by  the
respondent No. 2-School, which is an aided institution.
Respondent No. 1, who was appointed in 1997 by the
respondent No. 2-School, filed a writ petition seeking
regularisation along with the consequential benefits. The
Single  Judge  of  the  High  Court  dismissed  the  writ
petition. This has been reversed by the Division Bench of
the High Court, vide the impugned order. Aggrieved, the
present appeal has been filed by the State.
4) Merely because the respondent No.2-School is an
aided  institution,  one  cannot  say  that  for  every
1

## Page 380

unsubsidised vocational Instructor’s post, the appellants
are bound to pay the salary. What was earlier given by
way of concession vide GO No. 35 dated 09.02.2007 was
clearly a one-time measure. 
5) Additionally,  Section  14A  of  the  Tamil  Nadu
Recognised Private Schools (Regulation) Act, 1973 clearly
prohibits grant-in-aid for any additional post in any
class or course of instruction after the commencement of
the academic year 1991-1992 in a private school. It is
not in dispute that the course for which respondent No. 1
was appointed commenced only from the academic year 1992-
1993, for which no grant-in-aid for payment of salary to
respondent No. 1 could be made. So long as the said
provision is in the statute and in view of the settled
position of law, if an institution seeks grant-in-aid, it
is bound by the directions issued and the conditions
imposed.
6) In such view of the matter, we are not in a position
to approve the decision passed by the High Court vide the
impugned order.  
7) Accordingly, the impugned order passed by the High
Court stands set aside.
8) However, we note with concern that this entire
2

## Page 381

scenario has been brought about by the respondent No.2 –
School.  As this  Court has  already held,  in such  a
situation, a hapless victim, such as respondent No. 1 who
was appointed in 1997 and has retired in 2024, cannot be
made to suffer.
9) In such view of the matter, the respondent No.2 –
School, which despite being served, has chosen not to
appear before us, shall pay the salary and other benefits,
if any, to respondent No.1.
10) Accordingly, the appeal stands allowed.
11) Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

CIVIL APPEAL NO. 2520 OF 2024
YANKHOSAO ERUI & ORS. ...APPELLANTS
versus
ELOTHUNG KITHAN ...RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties.
2. This is a case wherein the suit filed by the respondent-
plaintiff for declaration of title along with other
reliefs, was dismissed by the Trial Court. The High
Court, vide the impugned order has confirmed the said
dismissal albeit on different grounds.
3. The short point that arises for our consideration in
this appeal is as to whether the High Court was right
in recording a finding that the suit property belongs to
the Kithan clan, while dismissing the first appeal.
4. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellants
submits that the impugned finding recorded by the High
Court, without even going into the evidence as regards
the same, cannot be sustained in the eye of law. There
is no admission on part of the appellants that the suit
property belongs to the Kithan clan.  After taking a
view that no evidence has been brought on record by the
plaintiff to establish exclusive title over the suit
1

## Page 384

land  and  that  since  the  plaintiff  has  avoided  the
witness box, the suit deserves to be dismissed, the
impugned finding ought not to have been recorded.
5. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  respondent
submits that as his appeal before the High Court has
been dismissed, the present appeal is not maintainable
and therefore, the impugned order needs no interference
by this Court.
6. We find force in the submissions made by the learned
counsel appearing for the appellants. The suit has been
dismissed, and we find absolutely no evidence, based on
which  the  impugned  finding  that  the  suit  property
belongs to the Kithan clan, has been recorded by the
High Court.  No representative of the Kithan clan has
been made a party to these proceedings as well.
7. Suffice it is to state that the impugned finding recorded
by the High Court is totally irrelevant, and even
assuming that it is true, it shall not have any bearing
on future proceedings, if any.
8. In such view of the matter, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned finding recorded by the High Court in
favour of the Kithan clan with respect to the title of
the suit property.
9. Accordingly, the impugned finding recorded by the High
Court is set aside, and the appeal stands allowed in
2

## Page 385

the aforesaid terms, with liberty to the parties to
agitate their contentions before the appropriate Court,
in accordance with law.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

## Page 387

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(Arising out of S.L.P. (C) No. 7706 of 2025)
KULDEEP THAPAR  ...Appellant
VERSUS
VIJAY KALRA & ORS.                ...Respondents
O R D E R
1) Leave granted. 
2) This is a case wherein the appellant was arrayed as
defendant  No.  2  in  a  suit  for  ejectment/possession,
permanent injunction and recovery of damages/mesne profits.
During the pendency of the suit, the appellant was deleted
from the array of parties even before filing the written
statement on his application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the
Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short, ‘the CPC’). The
suit was thereafter decreed by the Trial Court. Pending the
appeal against the same filed by respondent No. 1 being
defendant  No.  1,  the  High  Court  has  exercised  its
discretion in allowing the application of the respondent
No. 1 under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC seeking impleadment
of  the  appellant,  while  dismissing  the  appellant’s
application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the CPC seeking
deletion of his name from the array of parties, vide the
impugned order.
1

## Page 388

3) We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties. 
4) The object of Order I Rule 10 of the CPC is to
facilitate the Court to decide the lis before it. To
exercise the said discretion, there is no need for an
application per se. However, in the case at hand, the Trial
Court itself was pleased to delete the appellant’s name
from the array of parties. 
5) The principle of the plaintiff being the dominus litis
would apply, though the provision under Order I Rule 10 of
the CPC stands on a different footing.
6) We are concerned with a suit for ejectment, among
other reliefs. The application under Order 1 Rule 10 of the
CPC seeking impleadment of the appellant has been filed by
respondent No. 1, who is the original defendant No. 1 and
the appellant before the High Court. 
7) In our considered view, the appellant before us is
not a necessary party to the appeal pending before the High
Court as he is not required for deciding the lis. It is the
contention  of  respondent  No.1  that  the  appellant  has
received money from him and put him in possession of the
suit property. The said contention is not required to be
considered in the appeal pending before the High Court.
2

## Page 389

8) Also, there is a difference between a party being a
necessary one and a proper one. In our view, the appellant
is not even a proper party in deciding the lis for
ejectment. The question for consideration before the High
Court is as to whether the decree passed by the Trial Court
is correct or not.
9) In such view of the matter, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order passed by the High Court with
liberty to respondent No.1 to take recourse to law as
against the appellant before us.
10) Accordingly, the impugned order passed by the High
Court stands set aside, and the appeal is allowed in the
aforesaid terms.
11) Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
………………………………………………………J.
                      (M.M. SUNDRESH)
………………………………………………………J.

AUGUST 20, 2026.

exercise. Hence, after issuing show cause notices against the writ applicants
were terminated on 13.02.2024 on the ground of the selection process was
tainted, which was again challenged in Writ Application No. 5091/2024 the
jurisdictional High Court by Order dated 09.07.2024 stayed the direction issued

for alleged non-compliance of this order contempt proceedings were initiated

in the contempt proceedings, which is the subject matter of the present
appeals. Being aggrieved by the order of the learned Single Judge the State

## Page 412

filed writ appeal(s) in which stay was sought for and was not granted. Hence,

Contempt Court directed them to appear in person and framing of the charge,
the present appellants filed these appeals, this Court by Order dated
08.09.2025 stayed the further proceedings in Contempt Application (Civil) No.
640/2025 which is in operation till date. 
4.  Though several contentions have been urged and rebutted, the fact
remains that the writ application is still pending before the learned Single Judge.
Hence, continuation of the present proceedings would only be permitting the list
to be pending at all levels.  Hence, in such circumstances, we deem it apt and
proper to continue the stay which was granted by this Court on 08.09.2025, till
the disposal of the Writ Application Nos. 5091/2024, 2760/2024 and 2758/2024
and request the High Court to dispose of the writ applications expeditiously. It is
needless to state, in view of the aforesaid order, the writ appeal(s) as well as
the contempt application(s), would not survive for consideration and the
jurisdictional Courts can consign the same to records for statistical purposes.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
  CIVIL APPEAL NO.3330/2012
PUNNU RAM                               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
LATURIA RAM DEAD TH. LRS               Respondent(s)
O R D E R
We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the appellant and the learned Amicus Curiae.
The appellant before us is the plaintiff in the
suit. The suit was for mandatory injunction and
possession. 
The case of the appellant is that he is the
owner  of  the  property  and  he  permitted  the
respondent to use the property as a licensee.
A defence was taken by the respondent that there
is  a  tenancy.  In  support  of  the  defence,  the
respondent has relied upon the revenue entry in
which the respondent is shown as the ‘Gair Marusi’
of  the  appellant  that  is  the  tenant  of  the
appellant. The Trial Court accepted this revenue
entry and dismissed the suit.  There is no dispute
with regard to the said revenue entry.  The only
case of the appellant is that the entry so made was
wrong.  

## Page 436

2
The First Appellate Court was pleased to reverse
the judgment and decree of the Trial Court by
drawing an adverse inference against the respondent
on the premise that the respondent has not chosen to
step into the witness box.  Such view of the First
Appellate Court has been reversed by the High Court
inter  alia  expressing  its  agreement  with  the
reasoning of the Trial Court.
The learned counsel appearing for the appellant
submitted that as the respondent had not entered the
witness box, the High Court has committed an error
in restoring the judgment and decree of the Trial
Court and the evidence rendered by the plaintiff’s
witnesses was not taken into consideration by the
High Court.
We do not find any merit in this appeal.
The revenue records clearly indicate the fact
that the respondent was a tenant, from 1965 onwards.
In such case, there is no need for the respondent,
being the defendant, to step into the witness box.
The need to step into the witness would arise only
when a new fact which is asserted by a party is
required to be proved.
The appellant, being the plaintiff, must stand
on his own legs to prove his case. As a defendant,
it is well open to the respondent to take even
inconsistent pleas, which is not available in the

## Page 437

3
case on hand.
So long as the document is not in dispute and it
is the appellant who seeks to interpret it in a
different way which has not been found in his favour
by the Courts below, coupled with the further fact
that the revenue officers were neither made parties
nor were they examined in the present proceedings,
we do not find any reason to interfere with the
impugned judgment passed by the High Court.
However, inasmuch as the title of the appellant
is not in dispute as the very plea of the respondent
itself is one of tenancy, liberty is granted to the
appellant to initiate fresh proceedings in which
case the present proceedings will not come in the
way.
Accordingly, the appeal stands dismissed with
aforesaid liberty.
The able assistance rendered by the learned
Amicus Curiae is placed on record.
Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
………………………………………………..J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
………………………………………...….J.
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]
NEW DELHI;
AUGUST 19, 2026.

1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  gist  of  the  prosecution  case  is,  appellant
introduced the complainant and the other co-accused to
invest in business scheme with the promise of high returns
and there is a partnership deed also executed under which
the  complainant  is  said  to  have  paid  Rs.30,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty Lakh only) and subsequently, amounts had
been transferred to the co-accused. Hence, a complaint
came to be lodged against the accused for cheating and
luring him to invest in business with promise of high returns
and  in  the  process  complainant  had  lost  Rs.82,00,000/-
1

## Page 440

(Rupees Eighty T wo lakh only). It is during the course of the
investigation that the appellant was arrested and has been
in custody for more than one year and three months. On
conclusion of investigation, charge sheet has been filed. In
fact, the co-accused has been released on bail to whom the
complainant had paid the amounts. The present appellant
is said to have acted as facilitator of introducing the co-
accused.
4. In the light of these facts, we are of the considered
view  that  appellant  is  entitled  to  the  relief  sought  for.
Hence, appeals are allowed and appellant is ordered to be
released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional Court may deem fit to impose.

O  R  D  E  R
1. The  petitioner-wife  seeks  transfer  of  HMA/420/2025,
titled  as  Harjee  Gulati vs.  Ishwinder  Kaur,  filed  by  the
respondent-husband under Section 13(1)(i-a) of the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1955, which is pending before the Principal Judge, Family
Court,  Pathankot,  Punjab.  The  petitioner-wife  seeks  transfer

## Page 460

2
thereof to the Family Judge, East District, Karkardooma Court,
Delhi.
2. It  appears  that,  shortly  after  getting  married  on
27.10.2024, the parties started quarrelling and began instituting
cases against each other. It is, however, not in dispute that the
petitioner-wife is a resident of Delhi and it will, thus, be
extremely difficult for her to travel alone and defend herself in
the Divorce Petition filed by the respondent–husband at Pathankot,
which is situated at the extreme end of the State of Punjab. On the
other hand, the hardship, if any, likely to be caused to the
respondent-husband as a result of transfer can be adequately
compensated by permitting him to appear online, save and except
when his presence is required by the Family Court.
3. For the reasons aforestated, however, without expressing
any opinion on the merits of the case, the Transfer Petition is
allowed and HMA/420/2025, titled as  Harjee Gulati  vs.  Ishwinder
Kaur, filed by the respondent-husband under Section 13(1)(i-a) of
the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, which is pending before the Principal
Judge, Family Court, Pathankot, Punjab is ordered to be transferred
to the Family Judge, East District, Karkardooma Court, Delhi. The
records be forwarded to the transferee court forthwith. 
4. The Family Court may allow the respondent-husband to
appear online, save and except when his presence is required by the
Court.

ORDER
1. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  counsel  for  the  respondent-State  of  Madhya
Pradesh.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellant  takes  exception  to  the  order  dated
18.06.2026 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at
Jabalpur (briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting
the regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant  is  an  accused  in  Crime  No.697/2025
registered at Police Station- Kolgawan, District- Satna,
Madhya Pradesh under Sections 8A, 21 and 22 of the
Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 and
Sections 5 and 13 of the Drugs (Control) Act, 1950.
5. Allegation against the appellant is that a total of
810  bottles  of  Onrex  Cough  syrup  containing  codeine
1

## Page 468

phosphate were recovered from the two accused persons;
appellant and the other co-accused. From the possession of
the appellant, a total of 720 bottles were recovered which
is above the commercial quantity.
6. Appellant was arrested on 04.06.2025 and since then,
he has been in custody.
7. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that
appellant is a young person about 25 years of age. He has
already undergone custody for almost 01 year 03 months.
Insofar trial is concerned, only two witnesses have been
examined so far. Therefore, there is no possibility of
conclusion of the trial in the near future. Accordingly,
he submits that appellant may be enlarged on bail.
8. Learned counsel for the respondent-State of Madhya
Pradesh, on the other hand, has referred to the averments
made in the counter affidavit and submits that appellant
has another criminal antecedent being FIR NO.380/2025
registered before the same police station under Sections
115(2), 296, 3(5) and 351(3) of the BNS. He submits that
prosecution has cited a total of 23 witnesses, out of
which 02 witnesses have been examined, cross-examined and
discharged.
9. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, we are of the view that a case for
grant of bail is made out. As noticed supra, appellant is
in jail since 04.06.2025. There are 21 more witnesses to
be examined. The previous antecedent cited against the
2

## Page 469

appellant is of assault pertaining to grievous hurt.
10. Having regard to the above, the impugned order dated
18.06.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  is  set  aside.
Consequently,  we  direct  that  the  appellant  shall  be
produced before the jurisdiction Special Court within a
maximum period of 07 days from today, whereafter he shall
be released on bail on such terms and conditions as may be
deemed appropriate.
11. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.4345/2025
K.V. BHARATH                            Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
DREAMZ INFRA, INDIA PVT. LTD. & ORS.   Respondent(s)
O R D E R
We have heard the learned counsel appearing for
the appellant.
Despite notice having been served, including
the alternative mode, none appears on behalf of the
respondents.
By the impugned order, the National Consumer
Disputes Redressal Commission (hereinafter referred
to as the ‘NCDRC’) has rejected the application of
the appellant to implead the Promoter-cum-Managing
Director of respondent No.1 - Disha Choudhary as an
opposite party in the pending dispute.
Learned counsel appearing for the appellant, by
placing reliance on the decision of this Court in
Tejas J. Shah & Amisha T. Shah v. Mantri Technology
Constellations  Pvt.  Ltd.(Now  Known  as  Buoyant
Technology Constellations Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.  - Civil
Appeal Nos.4289-4290/2025 dated 27.07.2026, submits
that  the  liability  of  the  promoter,  being
independent, can go on, despite the moratorium being

## Page 484

2
applicable to the company. 
We find considerable force in the submissions
made  by  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
appellant.
In the case on hand, the impleading application
has been rejected by the NCDRC without issuing
notice and going into the issue as to whether there
was any improper conduct on the part of respondent
No.1.
Additionally, the respondents are not before us
despite notice having been served.
In the facts of the present case, we are
inclined  to  hold  that  the  application  for
impleadment ought to have been allowed by the NCDRC
and the contentious issues are to be heard and
decided thereafter. Such an exercise has not been
done.
The jurisdiction of the NCDRC is rather wide.
The rights conferred upon the consumer are also
rather  broad.  Thus,  in  the  light  of  the  facts
governing  the  instant  matter,  we  set  aside  the
impugned order and implead Disha Choudhary, who is
the Promoter-cum-Managing Director of the respondent
No.1 as an opposite party in the pending proceedings
before the NCDRC.

## Page 485

3
Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
All issues on merits are left open.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.
………………………………………………..J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
………………………………………...….J.

O R D E R
We have heard learned counsel for the appellant
and learned senior counsel for the respondent(s) on
caveat.
We fail to understand as to how the impugned
order passed by the National Company Law Appellate
Tribunal (NCLAT) could be questioned before this Court.
Termination of legal proceedings cannot be a
ground for assailing the same particularly when the
relief has also granted by such termination of legal
proceedings  viz.,  Corporate  Insolvency  Resolution
Process (CIRP) in the instant case.
Hence, the appeal is dismissed. However, the
amount deposited by the respondent herein could be
withdrawn  by  the  appellant  herein  by  filing  an
application before the NCLAT. If such an application is
filed, the same shall be considered in accordance with
law and the appellant herein is permitted to withdraw

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant petition has been filed challenging the order
dated 23.01.2026 passed by the High Court of Karnataka, whereby
regular bail has been declined to the petitioner. The petitioner is
one of the accused in FIR No.328/2022 dated 21.09.2022 registered
at  Police  Station  Kadugondanahalli,  Bengaluru,  under  Sections
153-A, 121A, 120B and 121 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (IPC),
1

## Page 496

inter alia, alleging a larger conspiracy by members of the Popular
Front of India to radicalise the youth and engage in unlawful and
violent activities. Upon completion of investigation, a chargesheet
dated 14.03.2023 was filed, invoking Section 153A and 120B of IPC
and Sections 17 and 18 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act,
1967 (UAPA). The petitioner was arrested on 22.09.2022 and has
remained in custody since then.
2. On the previous date of hearing, it was pointed out that the
prosecution proposes to examine more than 700 witnesses in the
pending trial. It was in such circumstances that we directed the
State to submit a prosecution plan, expressly specifying as to how
many protected witnesses are required to be examined. 
3. In deference thereto, an additional affidavit has been filed
by  the  State  of  Karnataka,  paragraph  6  whereof,  being  most
relevant, reads as follows:
“6. Furthermore, it is submitted that there are a total
of  707  witnesses,  out  of  which  64  are  protected
witnesses. In order to ensure their safety and to avoid
any delay in securing their presence at a later stage,
the Respondent-State proposes to examine the said 64
protected witnesses first. The Respondent-State would
ensure that the said 64 witnesses are examined within a
time-frame  of  One  year  so  as  to  facilitate  the
expeditious completion of the trial.”
4. During the course of hearing, we have outrightly rejected the
States proposal as contained in paragraph 6, especially when the
petitioner, as also statedly some of his co-accused, have been
incarcerated for almost four years. Faced with this, learned State
counsel has fairly submitted that the prosecution is willing to
abide by any directions that may be issued by this Court for an
2

## Page 497

expeditious trial. 
5. We are informed that there are three protected witnesses to be
examined qua the petitioner.
6. Learned counsel for the State has also pointed out that a
Special Court under Section 22 of the National Investigation Agency
Act, 2008 has been entrusted the trial in this case. In view of
successive orders passed by this Court in Suo Moto Writ Petition
(Criminal) No. 1/2026, we expect that such Special Court shall
exclusively try cases under the UAPA. Further, we deem it necessary
reiterate that all such exclusive Courts, including the Court where
the instant trial is pending, are expected to be assigned only 12
to 15 trials, which are to be dealt with on a day-to-day basis. If
such an arrangement has not been operationalised so far, we direct
the Union of India, the State of Karnataka, and the High Court of
Karnataka  to  take  necessary  steps  for  compliance  of  these
directions.
7. Keeping in view the attending facts of this case, we direct
the Judicial Officer presiding over the trial to firstly examine
the three protected witnesses qua the petitioner, followed by other
vital witnesses, to ensure that the material evidence qua the
petitioner is recorded within a period of not more than three
months. Upon doing so, the petitioner shall be at liberty to apply
for his release on bail afresh, and such an application shall be
considered as per its own merits, without being influenced by the
observations made in the impugned order.
8. Ordered accordingly. 
9. It goes without saying that the prosecution as well as the
3

## Page 498

defence will cooperate with the Special Court for expeditious
conclusion of evidence in terms of directions issued hereinabove.
10. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, disposed of.
11. All pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The petitioner  before this  Court has  filed the
present petition, being aggrieved by the impugned order
dated 11.02.2026 passed by the High Court of Judicature at
Allahabad in Criminal Misc. Bail Cancellation Application
No. 254 of 2025, whereby the High Court has cancelled the
bail granted to the petitioner.
1

## Page 507

2. The  brief  facts  of  the  case  reveal  that  the
petitioner was arrested in connection with FIR/Crime No.534
of 2024, registered at Police Station Kotwali Sadabad,
District  Hathras,  Uttar  Pradesh,  for  the  offences
punishable under Sections 103(1) and 61(2) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 and Sections 3/25/27 of the Arms Act,
1959.
3. The bail was granted to the petitioner vide order
dated  05.05.2025,  and  thereafter,  an  application  was
preferred for cancellation of bail.
4. The High Court in Paragraph 8 observed as under :
“This is the bail cancellation application
filed on behalf of the informant of the
case on the ground that opposite party No.
2 obtained the bail from this Court by
concealing the material facts and he did
not disclose his entire criminal history
and he is, however, having criminal history
of 13 other cases but he disclosed criminal
history of only one case and thus, he by
playing fraud obtained the bail order from
this Court.”
5. The other important aspect of the case is that in a
case of murder, bail was granted only after a custody of
one month and six days. The petitioner does have criminal
antecedents and there are as many as 13 cases, either
disposed of or in which bail has been granted to him.
6. In the considered opinion of this Court, the High
Court was justified in cancelling the bail by a detailed
2

## Page 508

and reasoned order, and, therefore, this Court does not
find any reason to interfere with the impugned order passed
by the High Court.
7. Accordingly,  the  Special  Leave  Petition  stands
dismissed.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

## Page 519

Bablu Sah and Mayank Kumar for their involvement in

Sah,  Shambhu  Sah  and  Ravi  Kumar  Sah.  In  the
chargesheet,  it  was  stated  that  investigation  is
continuing  against  Anjani  Devi,  Jyoti  Kumari  and
Rambha Devi (the present petitioners) and others. The
chargesheet  also  indicates  that  the  investigation
regarding use of XUV car is also continuing. 
2. It is the case of the petitioners that the
charge-sheeted accused were tried in Sessions Trial
No.812 of 2025. In that trial, all four accused  were
acquitted vide judgment dated 19.06.2026 passed by the
Court of District and Additional Sessions Judge-III,
Katihar. Besides, during trial, statement of Basanti
Devi (PW-3) was recorded. Therein she stated that her
son was sick and died a natural death, but, out of
anger, she lodged the F.I.R. against the accused
persons as despite demand of money for treatment of
her son, money was not provided to her.
3. The grievance of the petitioners is that despite
the  statement  of  Basanti  Devi  during  trial,

investigation against the petitioners has not been

          Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1

## Page 522

1. This is a complainant’s petition questioning the
reduction of sentence awarded to the respondents to the
period of sentence already undergone.  
2. The submission on behalf of the petitioner is that
there were as many as eleven injuries found on the body of
the injured including fracture of ulna and fibula bones.
Two of those injuries, though simple, were on the head. The
injuries were dangerous to life and, therefore, the High
Court ought not to have reduced the sentence of 5 years
awarded by the Trial Court to the period of sentence
already undergone while maintaining the conviction under
Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘the
IPC’).
3. We have considered the submissions and perused the
materials on record. 
4. What is clear from the nature of injuries that except
two injuries on the head, which were simple, rest were on
non-vital parts of the body. Therefore, it was doubtful
whether the accused, who had overpowered the victim, had
intention to kill him. In such circumstances, prima facie,
conviction  under  Section  307  of  the  IPC  may  not  be
sustainable.  However, since there is no appeal preferred
by the accused to question their conviction under Section
307 of the IPC, we do not wish to express any opinion on
that.  
2

## Page 523

5. However, having regard to the fact that the incident
is of the year 2000, and the High Court has already
enhanced the fine, we do not find a good reason to
interfere with the impugned order reducing the sentence of
imprisonment to the period of sentence already undergone
subject to deposit of enhanced fine.  
6. Accordingly, the special leave petition is dismissed.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
 (SHUBHAM SONI)                                 (SAPNA BANSAL)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

     UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the
following
                        O R D E R
1

## Page 552

IA No.11211/2026:
1. This application has been filed by accused No.2
(Yogeesha) for grant of bail by suspending the sentence
imposed on him.
2. The applicant – accused No.2 (Yogeesha) came to be
tried for an offence punishable under Sections 143, 148,
302, 201 and 114 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (“IPC”) in Sessions Case No.216/2012 and
acquitted  on  23.09.2016  for  the  said  offences  on
appreciation of evidence. The appellate court reversed the
said finding and convicted accused Nos.1 to 4 under
Section 304 read with 34 of the IPC, accused Nos.5 and 6
under Section 302 read with Sections 114 and 34 of the IPC
and accused Nos.1, 2 and 4 under Section 201 of the IPC.
The acquittal under Sections 143 and 148 of the IPC was
maintained. The trial court by its judgment of acquittal had
opined that the evidence of eye-witnesses PW-2, PW-3 and
PW-4 was unreliable and the prosecution had failed to
prove satisfactorily the motive and recovery of weapons.
The deficiencies in the eye-witnesses’ statements also
swayed in the mind of the trial court to acquit them. The
High Court by the impugned judgment after re-appreciation
2

## Page 553

of evidence was of the view that the eye-witnesses’
statements would establish their presence at the scene of
crime and they had also identified the accused. The fact
that there was no Test Identification Parade conducted
seems to have not been taken into account by the
appellate court. As to the actual motive for the incident
which weighed with the trial court is yet another factor
which requires to be examined by this Court in the light of
the finding arrived at by the High Court. For these
cumulative reasons, we are of the considered view that in
the light of divergent findings, the sentence imposed on
appellant – applicant (Yogeesha) deserves to be suspended
and enlarged the applicant – accused No.2 (Yogeesha) on
bail.
3. Hence, the application is allowed. The applicant –
accused No.2 (Yogeesha) is ordered to be enlarged on
regular bail by the jurisdictional Sessions Court on such
terms and conditions as it deems fit to impose. 
  (NEHA GUPTA)                      (AVGV RAMU)
COURT MASTER (SH)               COURT MASTER (NSH)

5. That Master Izyaan Ahmed aged about 12
years lives with the opposite party Ezaz
Ahmed and will stay with Ezaz Ahmed and all

the place where Master Izyaan Ahmed resides
or in any park or restaurant or mall nearby
1

## Page 555

as per the wish of Master Izyaan Ahmed and
out of which on one Sunday of the month Ezaz
Ahmed will allow her to meet Master Izyaan
Ahmed in Bulandshahar as per his wish from 12
PM to 5 PM.
2. In clause 6, it is stated that the days and time of meeting
Nazish Parveen will be changed as per the wish of Master Izyaan
Ahmed; it can be extended and after 1 year if Master Izyaan Ahmed
wishes, Nazish Parveen can keep him at night. 
3. Pursuant to our last order dated 17.08.2026, respondent-
husband has filed an affidavit where he has explained how he has
complied with the aforesaid terms of settlement. In addition to the
aforesaid, in paragraph 22 he has made the following offer:
The Respondent has, at all times, facilitated
the  child's  access  to  the  Petitioner  by
maintaining  open channels  of communication
and  even  providing   the  child's  personal
mobile number  so that coordination could
take  place  directly,  without  delay  or
interference. It is relevant to state that
the Respondent never obstructed communication
between the Petitioner and the child and, in
fact, went beyond the strict language of the
settlement  to  encourage  such  interaction,
while simultaneously respecting the child's
independence and emotional comfort.
4. We are of the view that the aforesaid arrangement can be
worked out by the parties. We direct the respondent-husband to
ensure that the son stays with the mother at least for minimum 2 to
3 hours on each of the meetings that they may have and she would be

respondent-husband to the Mall and drop him back after the meeting

relative.
5. List this matter after two months.

At this, the learned counsel has also referred to the order
dated 24.02.2026 passed by Registrar’s Court, whereby taking the
submission of the learned counsel for the petitioner that a report
had been filed by the Secretary/Commissioner, Registry was directed

would  continue  until  a  suitable  legislation  or
regulation framed by the State steps in.

determined the fee structure, which was notified on

legislation has stepped in, the interim arrangement

and the fees so determined could be realized from
the students for different courses.

copy of the first statutes and the ordinances, which

2. Based on the confessional statement of co-accused, Manish
Kumar, the petitioner, a jewellery shop owner, was accused
to  be  involved  in  a  gold-chain  snatching  incident.
According to the co-accused, the petitioner purchased the
chain from him and sold it in his shop. Accordingly, a
Supplementary  Charge-Sheet  No.670/2025  was  filed  on
31.07.2025, including the petitioner as an accused. The
Trial Court and High Court rejected the petitioner’s plea
for regular bail on grounds of his previous criminal
antecedents and gravity of offence.  
3. The learned Counsel for the petitioner submitted that there
was neither recovery of the case property made from the
petitioner nor is there any credible material on record to
establish purchase of stolen gold-chain by the petitioner.
It is further submitted that the three principal co-accused
in the case were granted bail by the trial Courts and the
High Court.
SLP(Crl.)  No.15205/2026                 2

## Page 604

4. On  a  prima  facie  consideration  of  non-examination  of
witnesses, the material on record and after hearing the
learned counsel for the parties, we are of the opinion that
the petitioner can be released on bail, subject to terms
and  conditions  that  the  Additional  Chief  Judicial
Magistrate-II, Danapur (the jurisdictional court) may deem
fit and appropriate to impose. Ordered accordingly. It is
further directed that, in the event the petitioner is found
to be involved in any future offence, of similar nature,
the bail granted to him shall stand cancelled.  
5. With the above directions, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967.  The allegations are that
the petitioner, along with his co-accused, is a member of the
Popular Front of India (PFI) and was indulging in unlawful
activities through provocative utterances and activities.
There are specific allegations that the petitioner was making
provocative speeches and promoting enmity and hatred among
different religious groups in India.
2. The petitioner was arrested on 22.09.2022 and has been
in custody since then. We are informed that the protected
witnesses  against  the  petitioner  have  already  deposed;
however, there are about 50 witnesses whose statements are
yet  to  be  recorded.   The  trial  has,  meanwhile,  been
transferred to the Special Court constituted under the orders
of this Court with the mandate that the pending trial will be
concluded in a year or so.
3. Taking  into  consideration  all  the  attending
circumstances, especially the period spent by the petitioner
in custody and the fact that the protected witnesses have
already been examined, we direct that the petitioner shall be
released on bail during the pendency of the trial,  subject
to such terms and conditions as may be imposed by the trial
court.  In addition to the conditions to be imposed by the
trial court, it is directed that the petitioner shall report
weekly to the jurisdictional police station and his contact
number and address shall always remain with the local police.
2

4. The Special Leave Petition is, accordingly, disposed of
with pending application(s), if any.

The petitioner is a victim and complainant in FIR No.429/20222.

made by her against her immediate superior who has considerable clout at
Udhampur and, therefore, she may not be able to get justice. Learned
counsel for the petitioner would however submit that the petitioner has
now been transferred to a place at Agartala, Tripura, and it would not be
therefore in the interest of justice that the trial is conducted at a Court at
Udhampur.

inclined to entertain this Transfer Petition and that too on the ground that
she has been transferred to a different place. If the petitioner has any

O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. At the outset, learned counsel for the respondent-State of
Maharashtra submits that, when the SLP was filed, there was a

## Page 753

2
SLP (CRL) No. 14939/2026
categorical  statement  that  the  petitioner  had  no  criminal
antecedents. When this was pointed out on the first day of hearing,
time was sought, and thereafter, a compilation of orders has been
placed on record showing that the petitioner has one other criminal
case against him.
3. Learned counsel for the petitioner was not able to satisfy the
Court as  to the reason why, at the first instance, when the
petition was filed, such disclosure was not made.
4. Having regard to the aforesaid and taking into consideration
the recent pronouncements by this Court with regard to the strict
view that the Court would take in such cases, where antecedents are
not  disclosed  and  the  consequences  thereof  may  lead  to the
dismissal of the case, we are not persuaded to entertain the
present Special Leave Petition.
5. At this stage, learned counsel for the petitioner submitted
that he may be permitted to withdraw the present Special Leave
Petition with liberty to file appropriate proceedings.
6. Accordingly, this Special Leave Petition stands dismissed as
withdrawn with the liberty aforesaid.

Trial Court.

Nair has executed the Will or not. In order to resolve the
controversy,  the  District  Judge,  Thiruvananthapuram  is

handwriting expert and a report be forwarded to this Court

## Page 787

SLP(Crl.)  No.10438/2026
1. It is shocking to note that the petitioner is in judicial
custody as an under-trial accused past eight years and six
months. Till this date, only six witnesses have been examined.
2. We would have definitely considered the plea for bail
only on the ground that the petitioner is in judicial custody as
an under trial prisoner past more than eight years, however,
what has deterred us in exercising our discretion are the
antecedents of the petitioner of the very same nature with which
he has been charged with in the presence case.
3. Let the trial proceed further expeditiously.
4. The Trial Court shall see to it that the entire trial is
completed within a period of six months from today without fail.
5. The disposal of the trial shall be informed to this
Court.
6. With the aforesaid, the Special Leave Petition stands
disposed of.
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

For Respondent(s) : 
          Upon hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. This Special Leave Petition impugns the order of the
High Court of Delhi dated 03.08.2026, by which, the High
Court declined to quash the First Information Report i.e.,
F.I.R. No. 320 of 2023 registered at PS: Greater Kailash,
District: South Delhi, and left it open to the petitioners
to seek appropriate remedy, in case a charge-sheet is filed
1

## Page 875

against the petitioners.
2. The submission on behalf of the petitioners is that
since the petitioners had invoked the jurisdiction of the
High Court to quash the F.I.R., the High Court ought to
have considered whether the F.I.R. was liable to be quashed
or not and, in absence thereof, the order of the High Court
deserves to be set aside.
3. To appropriately address the aforesaid submission, we
have  perused  the  F.I.R.,  which  has  been  annexed  as
Annexure-P1.  A perusal thereof would reveal that it
discloses commission of a cognizable offense. 
4. In such circumstances, the prayer to quash the F.I.R.
is  misconceived  and,  accordingly,  the  Special  Leave
Petition is dismissed.
5. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

We find that the learned Judge, having entertained the recall
application, directed the same to be listed on 17.12.2026 without
granting any interim protection. In his earlier Bail Application
No.3208/2024, the petitioner was granted interim protection but the
said bail application was dismissed for default by the learned
Judge on 28.03.2026. 
In that view of the matter, the petitioner shall not be
subjected to arrest till disposal of the recall application by the
High Court. 
In the light of this order, nothing survives in these special
leave petitions and the same are, accordingly, disposed of. 
We may note we have not gone into the merits of the matter. 
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of. 
SLP (Crl.) Nos. 16111-16113/2026
We are not inclined to interfere with an order of withdrawal.
However, liberty is granted to the petitioners, namely, Ajay
Sejwal @ Soni and Sikandar Singh Tandon, to seek recall of the said
order, if they so choose, highlighting the fact that they were
granted  interim  protection  in  the  earlier  anticipatory  bail
petitions which were dismissed. 
With the liberty aforestated, the special leave petitions are
dismissed.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

 UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                     O R D E R
1. We heard Mr. Mukul Rohtagi and Mr. Navin Pahwa, learned senior
counsel(s)  appearing  on  behalf  of  the  appellant  –  Corporate
Guarantor and on the other hand Mr. Tushar Mehta, the learned
Solicitor General appearing for the respondent – State Bank of
India.

## Page 929

2
2. We take notice of the fact that the National Company Law
Appellate Tribunal [in short, “NCLAT”] has admitted the appeal
preferred by the appellant before us, seeking to challenge the
order passed by the National Company Law Tribunal [in short,
“NCLT”] admitting the application under Section 7 of IBC preferred
by the State Bank of India.
3. In the said appeal, the appellant prayed for an interim
relief. Since two Members of the NCLAT differed on the issue
whether  relief  should  be  granted  or  not,  the  matter  was,
thereafter, heard by a third Member and the third Member has taken
the view that no case for grant of interim relief has been made out
by the appellant.
4. Manifold contentions are sought to be raised by both the
sides.  However, we take notice of the fact that the appeal is
coming up for hearing before the NCLAT on 10.09.2026.
5. If the appeal itself is taken up for hearing by the NCLAT on
10.09.2026, then we may not have to adjudicate the issues before us
on merits.
6. We would like to observe how well the matter is progressing
before the NCLAT on 10.09.2026.  It will be in fitness of things if
the NCLAT takes up the appeal for hearing on 10.09.2026, subject to
cooperation at the end of all the parties concerned.  
7. Post this matter on 15.09.2026.
